topic: Dickson Fjord megatsunami and seiche, Greenland 2023

slides.title: In September 2023, the whole planet started to hum.

slides.kicker: A signal no one could explain.
slides.body:
Seismometers from the Arctic to Antarctica picked up a strange vibration. Not an earthquake: one steady note, repeating about every 90 seconds.

Puzzled scientists called it a USO, an "unidentified seismic object".

slides.kicker: The clue came from a remote fjord.
slides.body:
On 16 September 2023, in Dickson Fjord, East Greenland, a mountain peak 1.2 km high collapsed.

More than 25 million cubic metres of rock and ice fell into the water. Enough to fill about 10,000 Olympic pools.

It set off a mega-tsunami. About 70 km away, 4-metre waves damaged a research base on Ella Island.

The fjord is on a common cruise route. Luckily, that day, no ships were nearby.
Hemmed in by steep walls, the water sloshed side to side about every 90 seconds. Each swing gave the Earth a tiny push.

It took a team from 40 institutions to link the hum to the wave. Their study appeared in Science in 2024.

In 2025, a satellite study confirmed it: the water surface had tilted by up to 2 metres, one way, then the other.

For decades, as the climate warmed, the glacier at the foot of the mountain had been thinning. It had been helping hold the slope in place.

Then, one day, it couldn't.

slides.lead: Slow changes don't stay slow forever.
slides.accent: They build quietly, then arrive all at once.

slides.line: Save this for the next time something seems fine.

caption:
In September 2023, seismometers around the world recorded a mysterious hum that lasted nine days. The cause: a landslide in Dickson Fjord, East Greenland, set off a 200-metre mega-tsunami that kept sloshing inside the fjord.

A glacier thinning for decades, then one mountain falling in a single day.

What slow change around you might be quietly building up?
